## 🎯 The task

Forecast your series with an **equal-weight combination** — the *Advanced Forecasting Methods* lecture —
and compare it with everything you have built before.

1. **Rebuild** your Lab 5 and Lab 7 models exactly as you submitted them, and check that they reproduce
   your earlier validation numbers. **Add MSTL** as a third candidate.
2. **Backtest** all three on four rolling origins, next to your benchmark.
3. **Combine** two or three of them — members chosen *before* you read the table — and read the table:
   would selecting one model have done better?
4. **Choose an interval**: the averaged bounds of the members, or a conformal interval from the
   combination's own errors — each judged on windows it did not see.
5. **Conclude** against your past results: your Lab 5 and Lab 7 scores on the hidden horizon, and what the
   combination is expected to add.

**Not this time:** plots of the series, decomposition, ACF and differencing. You have done them three
times; nothing in the rubric asks for them again. Every plot tonight is about the models.

- Two or three sentences: do the numbers match, and where does MSTL land next to your two models?

## 🎯 Section 2 — Forecast accuracy (3 points)

What you submit is **an equal-weight average of two or three members**, with an 80% interval from one of
the two recipes. No single model, no estimated weights, no model families beyond the three.

Scored from your submission file on the `h` observations after your history that nobody has seen:

$$
\text{skill} = \frac{\text{MASE of your forecast}}{\text{MASE of your benchmark}}
$$

| Skill | Points |
|---|---:|
| below 1 — you beat your benchmark | 3 |
| 1 to 1.1 — within 10% | 2 |
| above 1.1 | 1, and 3.3 must say why |

::: {.callout-note}
## What the pool guarantees, and what it does not

Measured on all 140 issued series, with **automatic** members fitted on the raw history — `AutoETS`,
`AutoARIMA`, `MSTL` — and scored on the hidden horizon:

| Forecast | Beats the benchmark | Within 10% | Worse | Median skill | Worst skill |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `AutoETS` + `AutoARIMA` | **100%** | — | — | 0.805 | 0.93 |
| all three | 96% | 3% | 1% | 0.798 | 1.18 |
| select the best of three on four windows | 96% | 2% | 2% | 0.811 | 1.23 |
| `MSTL` alone | 80% | 6% | 14% | 0.812 | 2.46 |

- The pool was screened so that `AutoETS` and `AutoARIMA` each beat the benchmark — so their average does
  too. **MSTL was not screened**: on one series in seven it loses by more than 10% on its own, and it can
  pull a combination with it. Whether it belongs in yours is a decision for 2.2.
- Your Lab 5 and Lab 7 models may not be the automatic ones. The table is about the automatic ones.
- **Intervals, on the hidden horizon:** the averaged bounds cover 78% of the months on average, the
  conformal recipe 79%; Winkler scores 3.75 and 3.85. Neither recipe wins in general — which is why you
  choose on your own windows.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Where this goes wrong

- **Choosing the members after reading the table.** Then the combination is a selection in disguise —
  the noisy decision it was meant to avoid. Write 2.2's note first.
- **Comparing on the validation window alone.** One window is one draw; the practice session's tourism
  case showed selection on three windows picking the test winner barely more often than a coin.
- **Judging the conformal interval on the windows it was built from.** It will look perfect. The
  template's `interval_check` leaves each window out in turn — use it.
- **Averaging forecasts on different scales.** Every member's forecast must be on the original scale —
  `fit_member` takes care of the log; do not exponentiate twice.
- **Forecasting from `train`.** The submission refits every member on the whole history.

📖 [FPP3 §13.4 Forecast combinations](https://otexts.com/fpp3/combinations.html) ·
[§5.5 Distributional forecasts and prediction intervals](https://otexts.com/fpp3/prediction-intervals.html) ·
[FPP3 §12.1 Complex seasonality (MSTL)](https://otexts.com/fpp3/complexseasonality.html)
:::
